citation: Muster's own policy for the config file, so the cases are the whole oracle. The key names it produces are the W3C UI Events codes in crates/muster-core/src/input/key.rs, generated from libghostty; the modifier bits are Modifiers in key_event.rs, whose numbering libghostty-vt's ABI fixes.
why: This is the one piece of Muster a person writes by hand, so every failure here is a config that looks right and does something else. Two things make that easy to get wrong. The first is spelling: a Mac user writes `cmd` and `opt`, a config carried over from elsewhere says `super` and `alt`, and reading only one of each pair leaves a file that silently does nothing. The second is that a chord's key is a physical key rather than a character - `cmd+shift+d` is the D key with shift held, not whatever shift+d produces on that layout - so the parse has to keep the modifier and not fold it into the key. Refusals matter as much: they name the piece that could not be read, because a config with one bad chord in twenty is one where `invalid keybinding` is not an answer.

cases.name: the ordinary one
cases.why: What most of the file looks like. `cmd` is the word on the key somebody is pressing, and Muster's own name for that bit is `super`.

cases.name: shift is held, not folded into the key
cases.why: The chord is the D key with shift down. Reading it as whatever shift+d produces would bind a different thing on every keyboard layout, and would come apart the first time somebody typed on a German one.

cases.name: every modifier under both of its names
cases.why: A Mac user writes one set and a config carried from elsewhere writes the other. Reading only one of each pair is a file that looks right and does nothing.

cases.name: the same chord in the words a Mac user reaches for
cases.why: The counterpart to the case above, and the reason both are pinned: these two strings have to end up identical.

cases.name: order and case are not part of the chord
cases.why: Nobody writing `Shift+Cmd+D` means something different from `cmd+shift+d`, and a parser that disagreed would produce a binding that never fires with no way to see why.

cases.name: spaces around the pieces
cases.why: Hand-edited files have them. Rejecting `cmd + d` would be a rule with nothing behind it.

cases.name: an arrow is spelled the way it is spoken
cases.why: The W3C name is `ArrowLeft` and nobody writes that in a config file. Both are read, and this is the half a person types.

cases.name: return and enter are the same key
cases.why: The key is labelled differently on different keyboards and means one thing. A config that used the other word and silently did nothing is exactly the failure this file exists to prevent.

cases.name: the wire's own spelling is still readable
cases.why: So a chord copied out of a log line or a corpus case can be pasted into a config and work. There is no reason to make somebody translate it.

cases.name: a bare key with nothing held
cases.why: Legal, and worth pinning as legal: somebody binding a function key on its own should not be told to add a modifier.

cases.name: the plus key, on the character the separator uses
cases.why: The one ambiguity in the format. A trailing `+` is the key rather than an empty piece, which is the only reading that lets `cmd++` mean anything at all.

cases.name: modifiers and no key
cases.why: Refused rather than bound to nothing. A binding that can never fire is indistinguishable from one that fires and does nothing, and only one of those is worth a message. What the message says is pinned in the driver rather than here, because prose in a corpus is a corpus that fails when the wording improves.

cases.name: two keys in one chord
cases.why: Sequences are not a thing Muster has, so `cmd+d+e` is somebody expecting something that will not happen.

cases.name: a key nobody has
cases.why: The commonest way a hand-edited chord is wrong: a name they guessed. The driver pins that the refusal quotes the piece it could not read and lists what is spellable.

cases.name: nothing at all
cases.why: An empty string in the config file, which is what a half-finished line leaves behind.
